The Jade Chapters describes the Biao horse as "fierce and brave," known for its speed and the small, speckled spots marking its coat. Among the Southwestern Ponies, those with this distinct red-dappled pattern are called Chibiao.
Legends from the Huayang Chorography tell of a divine steed that once rose from Dianchi Lake. Its offspring, known as "Dianchi Foals," were said to travel five hundred li a day. Later, during the Tang and Song dynasties, texts like the Book of the Man and the New Book of Tang praised the swift, high-tailed horses bred on the lush grasslands of the region, famed as "Yuetan Steeds." These Dian Horses, named for their origin near Dianchi Lake, are also known as Southwestern Ponies.
Small in stature, they have fine limbs, a short neck, a broad forehead, and firm, compact hooves. Prized for their endurance, they are suited for riding, pulling, and carrying loads, making them the most common breed in the southwest.
11087032746063964837:
Thirteen years ago, in the Dingwei year, during a time of chaos, the Khitan army invaded Kaifeng, unleashing fire and slaughter. The people rose to defend their homes, and after a month of bitter fighting, the invaders were repelled. As the city rebuilt, an old tree in the northwest was found scorched by the fires of war, yet miraculously sprouting new leaves. Seeing it as a divine sign of resilience, the people named it the Immortal Tree.
Later, when the usurper Liu Zhiyuan founded his short-lived Han dynasty, his sycophantic court seized upon this story. Claiming the tree as a heavenly omen, they forcibly expelled the local residents and built the Garden of Auspicious Omen, adorning its burnt branches with paper flowers to flatter their emperor.
And yet, what came of it? The Liu Han dynasty collapsed in just two generations. A dynasty's fate is not bound to trinkets and omens. How can a ruler in troubled times dare to cast aside caution for arrogance?
Now, in the first year of Jianlong, with the founding of the Great Song, the realm remains divided. Our Emperor, taking this tale of hubris as a solemn warning, has decreed that the garden be remade. It is renamed the Garden of Vigilance and returned to the people, a testament to his vow to rule with virtue, to remain ever-cautious, and to protect the nation and its people.
Decreed and erected in the seventh month of the first year of the Jianlong era

"In Shi Family Village, there were those called Flood Watchers. At Roaring Sands, there stood a drum: the Drum of Heavenly Vindication. A gash ran across its surface, a wound from the year 960.

That year, the Yellow River raged. The villagers beat the drum until it split, yet the Flood Watcher who should have returned with aid never came. At first, the drumming shook the skies, growing ever louder. Then, the wails of broken families and the frantic screams of children wove into its rhythm, until the drum could no longer drown out the crying. Finally, the weeping stopped. The drumming stopped. The weepers were dead. The drum was shattered.

The man the drum failed to summon was Shi Shouxin.

At the very moment the Drum of Heavenly Vindication shattered, his new lord donned the yellow robe of emperorship, escorted into Kaifeng. The ceremonial procession of the returning army was so thunderous that perhaps he truly could not hear the pleading drumbeats from his home.

He was no longer a Flood Watcher. He was Deputy Commander of the Imperial Guard, then Minister of Equal Rank, and later, Commander of the Imperial Guard. The people of Shi Family Village could not recall this long string of titles. To them, his identity had never changed. Villagers would look at his parents as they passed and spit, ""Our humble village can't hold a general. As for Little Shouxin? He's long dead!""

The gash that split the drumhead was the symbol of his own shattered spine. He was the notorious turncoat, a man who climbed to power over the bones of his kin and friends, one of the murderers of Zhu Yu. The unheeded blood and tears dried into a chasm of hatred.

Shi Shouxin never returned to Shi Family Village.

No one knows if, standing in the imperial court, seeing a winding river churn white waves, or reading official reports of a flood somewhere, he ever remembered a shattered drum. Did the roar of the flood ever fade from his ears? Or had it, for him, never truly sounded at all?"

In the northern reaches of Qinghe lies the village of Thousand-Buddha, so named for its people, all followers of the Buddhist faith. In the early days of Xiande, Buddhist fervor swept through Qinghe, and in this village, devotion grew ever more intense, bordering on madness. A wandering monk known as Miaoshan came to the village and declared, "Your worship is naught but hypocrisy." The villagers refused to heed his words and drove him away.
Not long after, heavenly fire descended like a blazing canopy, consuming the village in an inferno. Houses vanished into a sea of flames, and for ten miles, nothing remained but scorched earth—none survived.
Some years later, in the Jianlong era, as travelers passed the desolate ruins in the depths of night, one heard the sound of quiet weeping rising from the wasteland. He said to his companions, "Could these be the lonely spirits of the villagers, still unwilling to find peace?"
